Matt wants to build a chicken coop on a rectangular piece of land. The diagonal has a length of $x+6,$ one side of the rectangle has a length of $x,$ and the second side has a length of $a(x).$

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's consider the right triangle formed by two sides and a diagonal.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14243908/assets/ba2ba6039f294df10db14d592ecc03f301a483745dfab2758a8fdc7df8a2b7d8.png)

According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+6)^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{a}^{2} \\ {a}^{2} & =(x+6)^{2}-{x}^{2} \\ a & =\sqrt{(x+6)^{2}-{x}^{2}} \\ a & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12x+36-{x}^{2}} \\ a & =\sqrt{12x+36} \\ a & =\sqrt{4(3x+9)} \\ a & =\sqrt{4}\cdot \sqrt{3x+9} \\ a & =2\sqrt{3x+9}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's analyze the given polynomial:

$$
p(x)={x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-972
$$

The degree ($n=3$) is odd, and the leading coefficient (${a}_{3}=1$) is positive. Therefore, the polynomial has the following end behavior:

- $p(x)\to -\infty $ as $x\to -\infty .$

- $p(x)\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty .$

Only the graph $A$ satisfies these conditions.

earlier_parts.problem:
Determine which of $x=6$, $x=9,$ and $x=10$ is a root of $p(x),$ and use this information to write down a factor of $p(x)$ in the form $(x-r).$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        is a factor of $p(x)$

feedback.worked_solution:
The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we consider the numbers $6$, $9,$ and $10$ as possible roots. Let's check each of these values in turn.

- $x=6$ is not a root of $p(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(6) & =(6)^{3}+3(6)^{2}-972 \\  & =216+108-972 \\  & =-648 \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

- $x=9$ is a root of $p(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(9) & =(9)^{3}+3(9)^{2}-972 \\  & =729+243-972 \\  & =972-972 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- $x=10$ is not a root of $p(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10) & =(10)^{3}+3(10)^{2}-972 \\  & =1\,000+300-972 \\  & =328 \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the factor theorem, $(x-9)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

earlier_parts.problem:
The polynomial $p(x)$ can be factored as 

$$
p(x)=(x-9)\cdot q(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is a quadratic polynomial. Find $q(x).$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $q(x)=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}

feedback.worked_solution:
To factor $p(x),$ we need to find its other factors.

Because $(x-9)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-9)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-9)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $9$ | $1$ | $3$ | $0$ | $-972$ |
|  | $↓$ | $9$ | $108$ | $972$ |
|  | $1$ | $12$ | $108$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-972}{x-9}=({x}^{2}+12x+108),
$$

which means that

$$
{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-972=(x-9)({x}^{2}+12x+108).
$$

To see whether the quadratic polynomial ${x}^{2}+12x+108$ can be factored any further, we calculate its discriminant:

$$
{b}^{2}-4ac={12}^{2}-4(1)(108)=-288<0
$$

So, the quadratic polynomial ${x}^{2}+12x+108$ cannot be factored over the real numbers since its discriminant is negative. 

Therefore, the full factorization of $p(x)$ over the real numbers is given by 

$$
(x-9)({x}^{2}+12x+108).
$$

earlier_parts.problem:
The equation ${x}^{2}+12x+108=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q$, and solve the equation.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $p+q\,=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$,\,x=-6\,\pm \,\text{i}$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-2}}

feedback.worked_solution:
We first move the constant to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+12x+108 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+12x & =-108\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+12x & =-108 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2} & =-108 \\ (x+6)^{2}-36 & =-108 \\ (x+6)^{2} & =-72\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=6,q=-72,$ and $p+q=-66.$

Finally, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+6)^{2} & =-72 \\ x+6 & =\pm \sqrt{-72} \\ x+6 & =\pm \sqrt{-36\cdot 2} \\ x+6 & =\pm 6\sqrt{2}\,\text{i} \\ x & =-6\pm \text{i}\,6\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=-6+6\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}$ and $x=-6-6\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.$
